title: Bunyan in jail
hookLine: a tinker imprisoned for preaching dreams the story that becomes Pilgrim's Progress

cards: John Bunyan mends pots and pans for a living. He's a tinker, with a tinker's hands and very little schooling. He also preaches, without a license from the Church of England, and in his England that's against the law.
So he's put in the county jail in Bedford. He can go home, he's told, if he promises to stop preaching. He won't promise.
The months in a cell turn into years, and his family outside struggles without him. A man with a hammer and no pulpit now has neither. What he does have is time, and a pen.

teach.h: AS I SLEPT, I DREAMED A DREAM.
teach.b: Listen to how the book he's remembered for begins: "As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and, as I slept, I dreamed a dream."
Old editions carry a note in the margin saying what the den is: the gaol, the jail. From the first sentence, the book hints it was dreamed behind bars. The dream is The Pilgrim's Progress.
A man named Christian carries a heavy burden and sets out from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City.
On the way he meets characters with names you can't forget: Evangelist, who points the way, Obstinate and Pliable, Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Faithful, Hopeful, Giant Despair in his castle.
Bunyan writes plainly, and Bible phrases run all through his pages. Here's why the jail matters. Bunyan couldn't walk anywhere.
So he wrote a book that is nothing but walking: roads, hills, sloughs, valleys, gates.

teach.h: A STUCK MAN WRITES A JOURNEY.
teach.b: The man who was stuck gave readers a journey.
Long before him, the apostle Paul wrote letters from his chains. To the Philippians, from prison, Paul writes that what happened to him has "fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel."
Bunyan seems to have believed something like that about his cell. The waiting wasn't wasted. It became the dream.

how: Christians in different churches read The Pilgrim's Progress at home, aloud with children, or in study groups, following Christian's journey a few chapters at a time.

o: the guide in Bunyan's dream who points Christian the way
the giant who traps Christian in a castle of despair
the pilgrim who walks beside Christian to the end

games.q: Bunyan in jail — tap the pairs.

s: he was a tinker who mended pots and pans, with very little schooling.
Bunyan could have gone home by promising to stop preaching
he refused to promise, so he stayed in jail.
The Pilgrim's Progress opens with a dream
"as I slept, I dreamed a dream": and the den where he slept was the jail.

games.q: you're John Bunyan. the jailer says you can go home tonight if you promise to stop preaching. what do you say?
o: promise, and go home to your family.
promise, and preach anyway in secret.
games.why: Bunyan refused, and stayed. the book he later dreamed in a den, which the margin calls the gaol, became The Pilgrim's Progress.

practice: Think of a place where you feel stuck right now, a job, a hospital room, a season of life that won't move. In the quiet, let one line come about it: not a solution, just a line, an image, the start of a story, and hold it.
If you pray, bring the stuck place to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Evangelist. The character in Bunyan's dream who points the way, the first guide Christian meets on his journey out of the City of Destruction.

carryVoice: Your line: the dream in the jail. Even a cell can hold a road. Until tomorrow.
